works.title: Signatures of a Kondo insulator in a multilayer moiré Superlattice
works.abstract: Abstract Kondo insulators are paradigmatic strongly correlated materials, traditionally found in f-electron compounds. They originate from the hybridization between itinerant conduction electrons and localized magnetic moments, which opens a gap in the electronic spectrum. Two-dimensional moiré systems provide a new route to flat bands with strong electron correlation, which host localized moments at half filling. Here we report signatures, based on local conductivity measurements using microwave impedance microscopy, of a Kondo insulator in a moiré superlattice of monolayer WS 2 / bilayer WSe 2 , in which one WSe 2 layer carries flat moiré bands and the other dispersive ones. When both layers are partially doped with two holes per moiré unit cell in total, an insulating state appears when the moiré band contains less than one hole. The insulator becomes metallic above a certain threshold magnetic field, evidence for the singlet nature of the Kondo insulator, and the observed behavior is reproduced by a periodic Anderson model. Our results open a route to simulating Kondo physics in tunable moiré systems.

Room-temperature continuous-wave lasing-like emission from solution-processed bulk monolayer MoS2 thin films
works.abstract: Abstract Monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) are promising laser-gain media for their direct bandgap and strong excitonic effects. However, existing TMD lasers typically rely on mechanically exfoliated or high-temperature chemical-vapor-deposition-grown materials, with their atomic-scale thickness inherently limiting the available optical gain volume. Here, we report room-temperature continuous-wave lasing-like emission from solution-processed bulk monolayer MoS 2 (BM-MoS 2 ) thin films in whispering-gallery-mode (WGM) cavities. Using solution exfoliation and spray coating under ambient conditions, we produce area- and thickness-scalable BM-MoS 2 films composed of electronically decoupled MoS 2 monolayers separated by organic spacers. This layered architecture preserves the intrinsic monolayer excitonic properties while providing a tunable gain volume beyond that of an isolated monolayer. Integrated with WGM cavities, the thickness-scalable BM-MoS 2 films enable a balance between the quality ( Q ) and optical confinement ( $$\varGamma$$ Γ ) factors. Power-dependent measurements reveal key lasing signatures, including a threshold-like input-output crossover accompanied by linewidth narrowing at a pump power of approximately 1.4 nW, and pump-induced polarization selection. Solution-processable BM-MoS 2 thus offers a scalable gain medium for thin-film laser photonics.

Quantitative measurement of viscosity in two-dimensional electron fluids
works.abstract: Electron hydrodynamics is an emerging framework that describes dynamics of interacting electron systems as conventional fluids. Although evidence for hydrodynamic-like transport has been reported in a variety of two-dimensional materials, precise quantitative measurement of the core parameter, electron viscosity, remains challenging. In this work, we demonstrate that magnetoresistance in Corbino-shaped graphene devices offers a simultaneous ohmmeter and viscosometer capability, allowing us to disentangle the individual ohmic and viscous contributions to transport, even near viscous-ohmic crossover. In both monolayer and bilayer graphene, the effective electron-electron scattering rate scales linearly with temperature, deviating markedly from the T 2 dependence expected in conventional Fermi liquids. Instead, it is consistent with a recently identified tomographic fluid regime, theoretically predicted to be generic for two-dimensional electron systems.

works.title: The genetic landscape of canine tumors: Insights from the Canine Cancer Genome Atlas (CCGA)
works.abstract: The Canine Cancer Genome Atlas (CCGA, https://caninecancergenomeatlas.org/ ) is an open, accessible comparative oncology resource that harmonizes whole-exome data across 10 canine tumor histotypes. It aggregates 667 tumor-normal pairs with curated single-nucleotide variants, insertions and deletions, structural variants, and copy number aberrations. Cohort-depth stratification distinguished primary, exploratory, and descriptive analyses. Selection analyses identified 39 cancer drivers, including recurrent TP53 , PIK3CA , PTEN , SETD2 , MAP3K14 , and FAT4 alterations; copy number events included MYC amplifications and PTEN deletions. Direct comparison with matched human cancers revealed conserved and species-enriched oncogenic mechanisms, pathways, and therapeutic contexts. The CCGA standardizes alignment, variant calling, and annotation through consensus pipelines and provides downloadable data and interactive analyses. This reusable framework advances precision veterinary oncology and strengthens translational bridges to human cancer, supporting comparative and translational research.

works.title: Giant elastoresistance in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene
works.abstract: Strongly correlated and topological phases in moiré materials are exquisitely sensitive to lattice geometry at both atomic and superlattice length scales. Twist angle, pressure, and strain directly modify the lattice and thus act as highly effective tuning parameters. Here, we examined electrical transport in twisted bilayer graphene subjected to continuous uniaxial strain. Near the magic angle (≈1.1°), devices exhibited a pronounced elastoresistance that depended on band filling and temperature, with a gauge factor more than two orders of magnitude larger than that of conventional metals. In selected doping regimes, the elastoresistance exhibited a Curie-Weiss–like temperature divergence. We discuss possible microscopic origins, including nematic fluctuations and enhanced electronic entropy from fluctuating isospin moments. Our work establishes uniaxial strain as a versatile probe of correlated physics in a moiré material.

works.title: Limited genomic predictability of complex trait evolution despite genotype-phenotype stability
works.abstract: Whether genomic data can be used to effectively predict adaptation in natural populations is unknown. Here, we tested the efficacy of genomic prediction of complex trait evolution by monitoring genome-wide allele frequencies and pigmentation variation in genetically diverse populations of Drosophila melanogaster during evolution in both field mesocosms and a controlled, lab-based setting. At two points during trait evolution, we produced a high-powered, well-resolved genotype-phenotype map that exhibited marked stability across independent populations. Although we were able to use this map to correctly infer the direction of pigmentation evolution in both the lab and field settings, the particular loci responding to selection were largely unpredictable based on the direction of trait evolution itself. Our results hold implications for the promise, and limitations, of genomic prediction.

works.title: Increased demographic turnover and isolation precede social fragmentation in Asian elephants
works.abstract: Humans and many other animals live in interconnected social communities that are essential for survival and well-being. In principle, communities can persist despite changes in constituent members. However, gradually accumulating changes to membership could push systems past critical thresholds into alternate states, restructuring patterns of connectivity. Such changes can further affect systemic resilience against disturbance. We investigated social network dynamics for 443 wild female Asian elephants over 12 years by tracking community membership and structure. Following accumulated demographic turnover, networks fractured into smaller and more isolated communities. Connections changed not only owing to loss of members but also modifications in relationships among remaining individuals. This provides empirical evidence of a persistent state change in the social network of a long-lived terrestrial mammal following gradually accumulating demographic turnover.

works.title: TMEM184 proteins are Ca 2+ uptake transporters in lysosomes
works.abstract: Lysosomal Ca 2+ release from acidic stores is critical for lysosomal function, yet the molecular identity of the Ca 2+ uptake conduit has remained elusive. We used a Ca 2+ -imaging–based genetic screen of the lysosomal membrane proteome to identify TMEM184 family proteins as lysosomal Ca 2+ transporters (LyCaTs) essential for Ca 2+ uptake and refilling. TMEM184 selectively transported Ca 2+ while excluding monovalent cations. Loss of TMEM184B/C depleted lysosomal Ca 2+ stores, diminished Ca 2+ release, and disrupted lysosomal exocytosis, biogenesis, and membrane repair, thus phenocopying the release channel transient receptor potential mucolipin 1 (TRPML1) deficiency. Moreover, a human TMEM184B mutation associated with a neurodevelopmental disorder compromised lysosomal Ca 2+ transport, and Tmem184b -deficient mice exhibited profound motor impairment. Thus, TMEM184 constitutes the long-sought Ca 2+ uptake and refilling mechanism that governs lysosomal signaling and homeostasis.

works.title: Leading with humility
Poisoned hunting weapons, megafauna, and plant use at a 125,000-year-old Arabian paleolakeshore
works.abstract: After the African origin of Homo sapiens , multiple dispersals radiated into Asia, yet the Saharo-Arabian archaeological record remains sparse. In this study, we report on ‘Uruq Aljelibah, a Middle Paleolithic site dated to ~125,000 years ago (marine isotope stage 5e) and located on the shore of Mundafan paleolake, Saudi Arabia. Levallois assemblages, refits, and megafaunal associations indicate in situ tool production and carcass processing. Stone tool residues, use-wear, and biomarkers reveal animal and plant processing, including palms, tubers, trees, and shrubs. Several points exhibit impact damage and poison residues (from Acokanthera schimperi ), indicating use as hafted weapon tips within composite hunting systems. Megafaunal remains include hippopotamus, buffalo, gazelle, ostrich, and camel, illuminating hominin use of freshwater and grassland ecosystems.

works.title: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome outbreak linked to cruise ship travel in April–May 2026
works.abstract: In April 2026, a hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) outbreak caused by Andes virus (ANDV) occurred on a cruise ship. ANDV genome sequences were obtained for 10 of the 13 identified cases during a cross-country investigation established to share initial raw data for joint analysis with reciprocal quality control. The genomic data, symptom onsets, and plausible contact patterns strongly support a tightly linked outbreak cluster compatible with a single or very few zoonotic spillover events prior to embarkment followed by human-to-human transmission onboard. The outbreak represents the international displacement of a virus already known to be capable, under specific conditions, to transmit among humans, and does not suggest emergence of a unusual viral strain.

works.title: Climate aridity amplifies global riverine nitrate beyond human inputs
works.abstract: Nitrate pollution is widely perceived as a signature of human inputs. Here we show, with machine-learning reconstructed global maps, that climate aridity is also a dominant driver, systematically elevating nitrate concentrations across land-use gradients and creating unexpected hotspots beyond major agricultural and urban centers. Across ~2.9 million river segments worldwide, nitrate concentrations exceed ecological and health thresholds across ~33 and 2% of global land area, affecting ~5.6 billion (73%) and 0.5 billion (6%) people, respectively. Ecological threshold exceedance occurs mostly in headwaters, and about half of the health threshold exceedance occurs in middle-income countries and sparsely populated landscapes. These findings cast nitrate pollution as an aridity-amplified risk, suggesting that aridification may increase nitrate exposure even without additional human inputs. They call for regulatory standards that reflect risks across broad concentration ranges.

works.title: Geodetic observations in West Antarctica reveal geodynamically consistent 3D mantle viscosity
works.abstract: The rapid ice loss in West Antarctica since the 1990s has led to substantial ice surface lowering, regional bedrock uplift, and gravity reduction, as measured by geodetic observations. The bedrock (crustal) motions and gravity changes result from glacial isostatic adjustment (GIA), a process controlled by Earth’s viscoelastic properties and deglaciation history. In this study, we present GIA models with geodynamically consistent three-dimensional mantle viscoelastic structures and reconstructed ice history for Antarctica from 1900 to 2020, which explain both the observed Global Navigation Satellite System crustal motions and Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment gravity changes in West Antarctica. This study demonstrates that a mantle rheology including a weak asthenosphere and temperature-dependent viscosity is consistent with both mantle convection at million-year timescales and ongoing decadal GIA occurring in West Antarctica.

Differentiation of stem-like CD4 + T cells modulates early effector responses in colorectal cancer
works.abstract: Strategies to improve cancer immunotherapy have largely focused on the intratumor immunosuppressive microenvironment, whereas approaches to amplify peripheral T cells and promote tumor recruitment have not been thoroughly explored. Using imaging mass cytometry in patients with colorectal cancer (CRC), we observed T helper 1 (T H 1)–like immune architectures in mismatch repair–deficient tumors associated with response to anti–programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) immunotherapy. By contrast, mismatch repair–proficient (pMMR) tumors showed regulatory T–dominant spatial interactions. Clonal analyses revealed that stem-like CD4 + T cells differentiated into T H 1-like cells after PD-1 blockade. In pMMR CRC mouse models, combined OX40 agonist and PD-1 blockade suppressed tumor progression by expanding Il7r + early effector CD4 + intermediates in tumor-draining lymph nodes, promoting migration and connection with T H 1-like cells. This was accompanied by interferon-γ–dependent induction of immunostimulatory monocyte-macrophages and CD8 + effector T cells. These findings suggest that leveraging peripheral CD4 + T cell amplification may improve immunotherapy responses.

works.title: Carbon dioxide and amorphous water ices in the debris disk around β Pictoris
works.abstract: The star β Pictoris is orbited by a dusty debris disk, within which planet formation is occurring. The outer disk is sufficiently far from the star that volatile molecules are expected to freeze into solid ices. We observed the β Pictoris disk in the near-infrared using the James Webb Space Telescope. The spectrum shows features due to amorphous water ice (<7% crystallinity) and carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) ice in both the 12 CO 2 and 13 CO 2 isotopologues. We infer that the CO 2 ice is intimately mixed with the water ice at a ratio of 1:10. This implies that the ices formed in cold conditions, likely in the interstellar medium. Frequent collisions within the debris disk are required to explain the observed uniform distribution of icy dust grains.

works.title: A cellular atlas of the preinvasive breast cancer microenvironment
works.abstract: Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is the most common preinvasive breast cancer, however our knowledge of the DCIS tumor microenvironment (TME) remains limited. We constructed a comprehensive atlas of the TME in estrogen-receptor positive DCIS using fresh samples collected from normal breast tissues, DCIS and invasive breast cancers. We analyzed 854,911 cells from 159 patients by single cell RNA sequencing and 39 samples by spatial transcriptomics, which identified 9 cell types and 60 cell states. Our data shows remodeling of fibroblasts, vascular and basal cells that encircle the DCIS regions and immunosuppressive ducts that support the growth of the preinvasive cancer cells. This study delineates early alterations in the DCIS TME, including many changes that persist during invasive progression.

works.title: Early epidemiological and spatial assessment of the Bundibugyo virus outbreak 2026
works.abstract: A Bundibugyo virus outbreak was first reported on May 15th, 2026 in Ituri province, Democratic Republic of the Congo, with multiple cases reported across health zones during the early phase of the outbreak and suggestions of circulation weeks prior to detection. We pair highly resolved case and testing records with human mobility data to investigate the early outbreak dynamics of Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD). We show that human movement was a principle driver of early spatial expansion between May 10th and June 1st when the number of health zones and health areas reporting positive cases increased by 12 and 49, respectively. The early doubling time was estimated at ~10 days. Our work shows the rapid spatial expansion and growth of BVD with implications for intervention strategies.

works.title: ESCRT-0 condensation and cargo clustering drive extracellular vesicle budding from cilia
works.abstract: Cilia-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) mediate cell-cell communication and remove signaling molecules from cilia. The Hedgehog receptor Smoothened (SMO) is selected for packaging into ciliary EVs by ubiquitin chains, but how cargo selection is coupled to EV budding remains unknown. In this work, working in mouse kidney cells, we found that the ubiquitin reader endosomal sorting complex required for transport–0 (ESCRT-0) orchestrates both cargo selection and EV biogenesis. Unlike the conventional ESCRT pathway, SMO secretion did not require the ESCRT-III membrane scission machinery. Instead, ESCRT-0 condensed at the ciliary tip, where it clustered ubiquitinated SMO to drive EV biogenesis. Disrupting ESCRT-0 condensation blocked SMO secretion, and combining forced recruitment of ESCRT-0 with optogenetic clustering of SMO was sufficient to reconstitute EV budding. Thus, ESCRT-0 condensation and cargo clustering constitute a minimal module for ESCRT-III–independent reverse-topology budding.

works.title: A trapped catalytic product acts as molecular glue for innate immune signalosome assembly
works.abstract: Innate immune systems of living organisms are essential for host defense. Central to these systems is the Toll/interleukin-1 receptor (TIR) domain, an evolutionarily conserved module. From antiphage systems in prokaryotes to innate immune systems in plants, TIR domains have catalytic activity. However, TIR domains within animal innate immune receptors, such as Toll-like receptors (TLRs), have been considered as scaffolds for adaptor recruitment. We report that the TLR4 TIR domain possesses an allosterically activated nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD + ) hydrolase (NADase) activity that operates in a single-turnover manner. Its product, adenosine diphosphate ribose, is not released but entrapped as a “molecular glue,” stabilizing a composite catalytic pocket with adaptor TIR domain–containing adaptor protein (TIRAP) to nucleate signalosome assembly. This “produce-and-trap” mechanism represents a signaling mode that integrates enzymatic activity with adaptor function to drive downstream signaling.

works.title: Direct monitoring of breaching in deltaic submarine landslides
works.abstract: Submarine landslides threaten seabed infrastructure and trigger the transport of globally important amounts of sediment, carbon, and pollutants to deep-sea environments. However, fully submarine landslides have never been directly monitored in nature. Past hypotheses for their failure mechanism and dynamics therefore remain unvalidated for natural settings, including that prolonged upslope-migrating failures (breaching) occur in sandy seafloor environments. In this work, we present direct underwater monitoring of fully submarine landslides at Homathko Delta in western Canada that retrogress slowly upslope, indicating breaching-type failure. Their prolonged rather than instantaneous nature has important implications for the stress that seabed structures must be designed to withstand. Prolonged landslides also initiate sustained sediment flows (turbidity currents) that efficiently transport sediment, carbon, and pollutants further offshore.

works.title: Long-term local circulation of an Andes virus lineage in northern Patagonia is linked to the M/V Hondius outbreak
works.abstract: In 2026, a hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) outbreak caused by Andes virus (ANDV) occurred on a cruise ship. Analyses revealed an unexpected relationship to an outbreak in Argentina in 2018. Retrospective investigation clarified the 2018 outbreak could involve person-to-person transmission and a common ANDV lineage spanned HPS cases from 2018 to 2025 in a geographically defined area in northern Patagonia, without widespread community transmission of ANDV. Route reconstruction for the index cases in the cruise ship outbreak identified geographically plausible exposures to viruses of this lineage in Argentina, but their timing was inconsistent with the expected ANDV incubation period. The infection source for the cruise ship outbreak cannot be resolved with current information, highlighting the need to expand viral surveillance in the ANDV endemic region.

works.title: Tracking danger on the peaks
works.abstract: The Earth is warming, but not all regions are warming equally. In high mountain areas, temperatures are generally increasing by 1.5 to 2 times the global average, sometimes with devastating consequences. A small or gradual change in the mountain cryosphere—perhaps progressive thawing of frozen ground or a flood from a small glacial lake—can suddenly turn into a cascade of catastrophes with enormous ramifications. Monitoring systems for the cryosphere in high mountain areas have traditionally been designed to look at individual components and changes. What are the temperature and depth of the permafrost, or how much area is covered by snow, and what is the related avalanche danger? Many of the monitoring and warning systems were designed for historical patterns of snowfall or rainfall, and a river gauge may no longer be adequate if there is greater flow in the rainy season, or increased sediment that could damage the gauge.

works.title: The cryosphere beyond a planetary safe operating space
works.abstract: The cryosphere plays a vital role in regulating planetary dynamics and habitability, yet it remains unclear whether its essential functions remain within a safe operating space (SOS) amid Anthropocene change. Here, we propose a cryosphere SOS and systematically evaluate its contributions to Earth system resilience using the planetary boundaries framework. Multiple lines of evidence indicate an accelerating and partly irreversible loss of cryospheric integrity, driven by amplifying feedbacks. Key cryospheric control variables either have left or are committed to departing from Holocene-like conditions. We conclude that the cryosphere has breached its SOS and is on a trajectory that locks in long-term risks for human societies and ecosystems. Safeguarding planetary resilience therefore requires explicit consideration of cryosphere change and its interactions across the Earth system.

works.title: Atmospheric O 2 reveals a strengthening ocean carbon sink and a stagnant net land sink since 1990
works.abstract: The global ocean and land biosphere absorb roughly half of fossil fuel carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) emissions. The temporal evolution of these sinks remains difficult to quantify owing to data sparsity. Leveraging 30+ years of atmospheric oxygen (O 2 ) and CO 2 observations, we find that the ocean carbon sink increased by 0.63 ± 0.19 petagrams of carbon per year per decade (Pg C year −1 decade −1 ) (a mean of 2.8 ± 0.4 Pg C year −1 ), accounting for 35% of fossil emissions between 1990 and 2019. The net land sink shows no robust trend (with a mean of 1.0 ± 0.5 Pg C year −1 , accounting for 13% of fossil emissions), despite large decadal variability. These results challenge many process-based model simulations of the land and ocean sinks, questioning their ability to accurately predict future climate states.

works.title: Ebola vaccine lessons
The quantum agreement theorem
works.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
works.abstract: Intersubjective consistency asks when different observers of a physical system, reasoning from a shared theory, will agree on their probability assessments. Classical probability theory provides a benchmark in the form of the Agreement Theorem [R. J. Aumann, Ann. Stat. 4 , 1236–1239 (1976)]. We study the quantum mechanics (QM) analog to the classical Agreement Theorem in a finite-dimensional tripartite setting in which two observers obtain information via local projective measurements. We represent their mutual awareness by common certainty, which is formally an infinite hierarchy of certainty operators concerning the probability of an event of interest. We first prove that if the observers’ measurements commute with one another and with the property of interest, common certainty forces their probability assessments to coincide, thereby recovering a QM analog to the classical Agreement Theorem. We then construct a one-parameter family of qutrit–qubit–qubit models in which one observer’s measurement does not commute with the property and common certainty of disagreement occurs—a distinctively QM phenomenon. The mechanism is coherence between branches distinguished by one but not the other observer’s measurement. When measurement outcomes are stored in a classical register, the resulting dephasing removes this coherence and restores agreement. Finally, we prove that QM does not permit the extreme 0 - 1 configuration in which Alice is certain of a property and is also certain that Bob is certain of its negation. These results aim to turn debate in QM about observer-dependent facts into precise mathematical conditions for when intersubjective agreement or disagreement in QM can be sustained.

works.title: Quantifying the hierarchical topological decay of fluid knots
works.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
works.abstract: In this paper we analyze the hierarchical topological cascade of knotted and linked filaments associated with the natural decay of superfluid vortex tangles. This is done by using an algebraic reformulation of knot polynomial invariants to quantify the topological states of the cascade process. By interpreting the evolutionary paths associated with vortex knot dynamics as geodesic flows in an appropriate knot polynomial space defined by adapted Jones polynomials [X. Liu, R. L. Ricca, J. Phys. A Math. Theor. 45 , 205501 (2012).], we introduce an entanglement index to quantify the probability density of occurrence of each topological state. By this method we analyze all prime knots, links, and composites up to 8 crossings, and show that this measure detects accurately the decreasing topological complexity observed in simulations and laboratory experiments. By a comparative analysis carried out with data based on an alternative measure (complexity degree), we show that this entanglement index proves to be a more robust and reliable quantifier. The theoretical framework proposed here can be applied to other types of physical systems, where networks of filamentary structures are subject to continuous topological change and reorganization.

works.title: The p38α MAPK–MK2 axis drives chemotherapy-mediated nuclear actin remodeling to promote ovarian cancer progression
works.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
works.abstract: Nuclear F-actin facilitates DNA damage repair and contributes to cancer chemoresistance. However, the regulatory mechanisms controlling its dynamic polymerization in response to genotoxic stress remain poorly defined. A major barrier in nuclear actin research is the lack of tools for precise, high-throughput analysis. To systematically investigate nuclear F-actin assembly in DNA damage response, we developed a deep learning pipeline, named nFANet, for high-throughput detection and analysis of nuclear F-actin. Here, using ovarian cancer—a malignancy where chemoresistance is a major clinical obstacle—as a model, we showed that platinum-based chemotherapy robustly induces nuclear F-actin assembly. A subsequent kinome screening, in combination with the application of nFANet, identified the kinase p38α MAPK as a critical upstream regulator of platinum-induced nuclear F-actin assembly. Mechanistically, the p38α MAPK–MK2 signaling pathway promotes formin-mediated nuclear F-actin assembly in response to chemotherapy. Importantly, pharmacological inhibition or genetic knockout of the p38α MAPK–MK2 pathway sensitized ovarian cancer cells to platinum-based therapy. Our work uncovers a key mechanism governing nuclear actin remodeling under genotoxic stress and lays the foundation for identifying a patient subgroup likely to benefit from therapeutic targeting of this pathway.

works.title: Synergy between Gq and Gi proteins for the antipsychotic-like effects of mGlu2 receptors
works.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
works.abstract: The capacity of one G protein–coupled receptor (GPCR) to modulate signaling outputs of another is a phenomenon with potential implications for neuron function and therapeutic action. Notably, Gi/o-coupled receptors have been shown to generate calcium signals after costimulation of Gq-coupled receptors, an effect resulting from a crosstalk between signaling cascades. But the relevance for brain function and for therapeutic applications remains largely unclear. Here we show that Gi/o-coupled metabotropic glutamate 2 (mGlu2) receptors can generate calcium signals in neurons. It results from either agonist activation or constitutive activity of a Gq-coupled receptor endogenously coexpressed with mGlu2, independently of dimerization. Specifically, the constitutively active platelet-activating factor receptor (PAFR) plays an essential role in mGlu2-calcium signaling in hippocampal neurons, an effect largely inhibited by PAFR inverse agonists and genetic variants. This mGlu2-PAFR crosstalk is required for the cognitive and behavioral rescue produced by mGlu2 agonists in a mouse model of NMDA receptor hypofunction. These data highlight the complexity of GPCR signaling and provide key insights on therapeutic strategies for psychiatric disorders.

works.title: Diffusional depth profiling using electrochemiluminescence microscopy
works.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
works.abstract: Electrochemiluminescence (ECL) microscopy has emerged as a powerful 2D imaging technique with exceptional spatial resolution, enabling visualization of biological entities, nanomaterials, and multiphase systems. Conventional ECL experiments rely on coreactant concentrations in large excess of the luminophore to generate a bright signal in the vicinity of the electrode. While effective for surface interrogation, this confinement limits resolution in the z-dimension, making 3D imaging challenging. Here, we show that introducing an excess of luminophore enables access to 3D information through diffusion of the emission layer away from the electrode. By tuning the concentration ratio of tris(2,2’-bipyridine)ruthenium(II) ([Ru(bpy) 3 ] 2+ ) to tri-n-propylamine (TPrA), we control emission layer diffusivity. Initially, ECL arises from heterogeneous oxidation of both species at the electrode. As TPrA is depleted, the mechanism shifts to chemiluminescence, where [Ru(bpy) 3 ] 3+ oxidizes TPrA, generating a diffusing emissive layer that extends in the z-direction over time. Simulations and scanning electrochemical microscopy capture these diffusion profiles and highlight the role of concentration ratios. We apply this “diffusional depth profiling” to spirulina algae and spheroid cell models, insulating bodies that block light coming from the evolving emissive layer, revealing 3D morphology. This work uncovers the important influence of time and concentration on ECL emission layer expansion for depth profiling micro-to-mesoscale entities across biology and materials science.

works.title: scMomer: a pretraining framework for inferring robust cellular representations from single-cell transcriptomes
works.abstract: Abstract Foundation models offer new opportunities to capture cellular behavior from large-scale single-cell data. However, their development has been greatly constrained due to the limited availability of multi-omics profiles. Consequently, most models are designed for a single modality (e.g. scRNA-seq, or scATAC-seq, etc.), restricting their ability to capture the diversity of heterogeneous biological systems. Here, we introduce scMomer, a modality-aware pretraining framework designed for multi-modal representation learning under missing modality conditions. scMomer adopts a three-stage pretraining strategy that learns unimodal cell representations, models joint representations from multi-omics data, and distills multi-modal knowledge to enable multi-omics-like representations from unimodal input. Its modality-specific architecture and three-stage pretraining strategy enable effective learning under missing modality conditions and help capture cellular heterogeneity. Through extensive experiments, scMomer generates biologically meaningful embeddings and outperforms state-of-the-art unimodal approaches across diverse gene-level and cell-level downstream tasks, including cross-modality translation, gene function prediction, cell annotation, drug response prediction, and perturbation prediction. Overall, these results demonstrate that scMomer serves as a robust, generalizable, and scalable foundation for single-cell multi-modal analysis under missing modality conditions.

works.title: Evolution of the molybdenum and vanadium cycles through time and their impact on ancient nitrogen fixation
works.abstract: Abstract Biological nitrogen (N 2 ) fixation is crucial for incorporating atmospheric N 2 into the biosphere. However, the evolutionary trajectory of this process remains enigmatic, particularly regarding the paradoxical relationship between the presumed scarcity of molybdenum (Mo) in the Archean ocean—before oxidative weathering on land—and the apparent early emergence of Mo-based nitrogenase over the vanadium (V)-based alternative. Here, we integrate partitioning experiments with an extensive analysis of iron (Fe)-rich sediments through time to elucidate the behavior of Mo and V in ancient seawater. Our findings suggest that in the Archean to Paleoproterozoic, dissolved V was more efficiently removed from the water column than Mo, primarily due to the preferential incorporation of V into banded iron formations (BIF). Our data also suggest that dissolved Mo was more available in seawater than commonly assumed and that the ratio Mo/V was higher in the Archean than it is today. Higher Mo abundances and greater availability of Mo relative to V offers a compelling explanation for the earlier evolution of Mo-based nitrogenase over the alternative nitrogenases.

works.title: Scaling medical imaging report generation with multimodal reinforcement learning
works.abstract: Abstract In medical imaging report generation, supervised fine-tuning can overfit to superficial patterns and generalize poorly across institutions. We introduce Universal Report Generation (UNIRG), which adopts reinforcement learning to directly optimize clinically meaningful quality criteria. With this framework, we developed UNIRG-CXR, an 8-billion-parameter vision–language model trained on four public datasets (MIMIC-CXR, CheXpert Plus, ReXGradient-160k and IU-Xray) by supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning (group-relative policy optimization) against a composite lexical, semantic and clinical-error reward. We evaluated held-out test sets and an external proprietary dataset, with RadCliQ as primary metric and expert radiologist validation. Here we show that our method improves report quality and generalization: UNIRG-CXR surpasses prior models on the ReXrank benchmark across four datasets and two generation settings, exceeding the previous best score by over 50% on two test sets, and produces fewer clinically significant errors while maintaining performance on unseen data sources and across demographic subgroups.

works.title: SIP-enabled multi-omics reveals soil microbiome responses to drought and rehydration
works.abstract: Abstract The activity of the soil microbiome, and its balance of anabolic (organic C consuming) and catabolic (CO 2 -releasing) reactions, determines the magnitude and direction of soil carbon fluxes. Over half a century of research has revealed that soil water dynamics are key controllers of microbial activity. With increasing hydroclimate volatility expected across many regions of the Earth, there is a greater need to describe and quantify microbial responses to drought and rehydration cycles. In this study, we conducted rainfall exclusion experiments at two archetypical Mediterranean-type field sites. After rainfall exclusion and subsequent soil rehydration, we applied a SIP-enabled, multi-omics methodology to generate a multi-faceted case study of microbial growth, greenhouse gas fluxes, and the forms of carbon that drive both. Our results indicate that rehydration increases microbial anabolic processes by orders of magnitude, shifting cell generation times from years to days within just minutes. High-intensity drought increases the lag period before microbial growth resumes, but both stable-isotope probing and metagenomic inference agree that microbial communities exhibit greater capacity for rapid growth following drought stress. Furthermore, significant shifts in the soil metabolome are observed following drought and rehydration, implicating specific osmolytes as key to the microbial response and indicating metabolite diversity as a key modulator of microbiome functioning. Together, our results provide constraints on microbial activity rates in soil and mechanisms underpinning microbial responses to drought and rewetting. These findings motivate further research into microbial responses under increasingly volatile hydroclimate regimes and downstream contributions to the global carbon cycle. Significance Statement Soil is a major global store and source of carbon. The microbiome determine the fate of soil organic carbon, and the microbiome is ultimately controlled by soil water dynamics. Early, innovative experiments by H.F. Birch defined “The Birch Effect” – the observation that soils emit CO 2 following drying and subsequent rehydration. However, it remains unclear when, and to what magnitude, soil microorganisms are actively growing following this rehydration, and what biological mechanisms explain the observed CO 2 pulse. In this work, we apply an array of methodologies to address this question, describing rates of microbial growth during drought and rewetting. Our results provide crucial insights into how soil microbiomes will respond to increasing hydroclimate volatility across the globe.

works.title: Engineering CAR-Vδ2 T cells to boost persistence and anti-tumor function
works.abstract: Abstract Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-modified Vδ2 T cells are an attractive therapeutic cell platform for cancer immunotherapy. However, their clinical efficacy is limited by short in vivo persistence due to insufficient cytokine support and high susceptibility to activation-induced cell death (AICD). Through comparison of membrane-bound (mb) cytokines, we identified mbIL-18 to support superior anti-tumor activity of CAR-Vδ2 T cells in vitro and in vivo . To reduce constitutive surface exposure of IL-18 and enable antigen-driven signal 3, we fused MyD88 - the key IL-18R signaling mediator - to an extracellular domain of Fas (Fas88). Antigen stimulation-induced FasL engagement of Fas88 triggered IL-18 signaling while simultaneously protecting Vδ2 T cells from AICD. Fas88-armed human CAR-Vδ2 T cells produced superior yet stimulation-dependent in vivo expansion and functional persistence in xenograft models of hematologic and solid malignancies. Together, these findings highlight the importance of IL-18 signaling and AICD resistance for CAR-Vδ2 T cell activity, enabling a single-transgene modification to limit inflammatory risk and facilitate clinical translation.

works.title: A single NLS directs AGO1 import shaping small RNA loading and silencing outputs in Arabidopsis
works.abstract: Abstract Small RNAs (sRNAs) regulate plant development, stress responses and genome stability by guiding ARGONAUTE (AGO) proteins to their targets. AGO1 is the major effector of microRNA (miRNA) and 21/22-nucleotide (nt) secondary small interfering RNA (siRNA) pathways in Arabidopsis thaliana. However, how AGO1 subcellular dynamics shape sRNA loading and silencing remained unclear. Here, we validate a functional nuclear localization signal (NLS) in the N-terminal extension of AGO1 and identify IMPORTIN α2 (IMPα2) as a nuclear import factor acting within a larger importin α network. Using engineered nuclear-only and cytoplasmic-only AGO1 variants, we show that exclusive cytoplasmic AGO1 allows full miRNA target repression and secondary siRNA production in ago1 mutants, whereas nuclear-retained AGO1 only partially rescues miRNA function and exerts a dominant-negative effect on secondary siRNA biogenesis. sRNA immunoprecipitation assay reveals that miRNAs are preferentially loaded into AGO1 in the nucleus, while tasiRNA loading predominantly occurs in the cytoplasm. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that AGO1 spatial partitioning itself quantitatively shapes the efficiency and specificity of sRNA loading and the silencing outputs.

works.title: Phylogeographic and functional assembly of population-level bacterial immunity
works.abstract: Bacterial pangenomes provide a shared reservoir of antiphage defenses, yet the ecological and functional constraints shaping this reservoir remain unclear. Here, we combine comparative genomics of 206 Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae (Xoo) genomes with cross-infection assays of 50 strains against 36 phages and heterologous expression of 24 defense systems in a phage-sensitive Xoo chassis. The Xoo pan-defensome comprises a conserved core of 9 subtypes and a variable layer of 35 accessory and cloud subtypes structured by host phylogeography. Phages are more infectious on sympatric than allopatric hosts, consistent with local adaptation. Variable systems show stronger apparent activity than core systems, whereas resistance breadth is not predicted by defense system number. Co-expression of representative co-occurring and mutually exclusive system pairs reveals synergistic and antagonistic interactions underlying non-random repertoire assembly. Together, these findings extend the pan-immunity framework by showing that population-level immune reservoirs are shaped by both ecological structure and functional compatibility. In this study, the authors use comparative genomics and cross-infection assays to show a spatially and evolutionarily structured bacterial immune reservoir in which interactions among defense systems can reinforce or undermine phage resistance, refining the pan-immunity framework.

works.title: Autapse-inspired neuromorphic hardware with synapse–neuron integration for bidirectional feedback control
works.abstract: Abstract Establishing autonomous and energy-efficient feedback control at the hardware level remains challenging because conventional systems rely on centralized processing and continuous external computation, increasing energy consumption and system complexity. Here we show a neuromorphic autapse-inspired system that enables localized and bidirectional feedback control, using thermoregulation as a representative application. An autapse is a self-synaptic connection in which a neuron feeds its output back to its own synaptic input, enabling intrinsic feedback modulation. The system integrates a solid electrolyte-based synaptic transistor capable of multiplexing multiple inputs and a bidirectional leaky integrate-and-fire artificial neuron. By feeding the neuronal output back to an additional synaptic gate, excitatory and inhibitory feedback loops are realized within a compact architecture. Using an artificial thermoregulation platform, temperature-dependent inputs bidirectionally modulate neuronal firing frequency, demonstrating biologically inspired feedback control with a compact set of neuromorphic devices for autonomous and energy-efficient systems.

works.title: Structural basis of ligand-mediated transition to higher-order rubisco assemblies
works.abstract: Abstract Proteins often assemble as higher order complexes, underlying a diversity of molecular structures and biological functions. The emergence of protein-protein interactions between binding partners is generally considered to be the primary driver of oligomerization. However, ligand binding has also been demonstrated to affect higher-order assembly, though this phenomenon is not widely considered as a primary driver of oligomerization. Here, we describe the mechanism by which different rubisco oligomeric states are induced via ligand binding. By expanding the phylogenetic sampling of a unique clade of rubisco, we discover a range of oligomeric responses to ligand binding across the phylogeny and identify the structural features responsible for shifts in the oligomeric state that ultimately provide a path to evolving new quaternary structures. Here, we identify a ligand-dependent mechanism giving rise to new protein assemblies, in contrast with the typical process of evolving new protein-protein interfaces directly. Our findings describe a means by which binding and entrenchment of a ligand enables an increase in structural complexity.

works.title: Thin-film lithium niobate waveguide-integrated p-i-n Tungsten selenide photodiodes with 10Gbit/s data reception
works.abstract: Abstract Thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) is a promising photonic platform in next-generation integrated optoelectronics and on-chip/chip-chip interconnection due to its attractive optical property and versatility. However, integration of conventional-material-based photodetectors on TFLN platforms still faces multiple challenges. Herein, a high-bandwidth TFLN-based waveguide-integrated lateral WSe 2 p-i-n photodetector is presented. The localized self-aligned doping process eliminates slow carrier diffusion and defect trapping in doped regions which further boosts modulation bandwidth. Secondly, n-type and p-type Ohmic contacts, along with a high-quality p-n junction, are achieved through Se vacancy defect engineering and high-work function molybdenum oxide buffer layer, respectively. Furthermore, combined with the high dielectric constant of lithium niobate suppressing ionized impurity scattering, carrier mobilities exceeding 350 cm 2 /V·s are achieved for both electrons and holes, significantly accelerating carrier drift. The device features a measured bandwidth of 1.12 GHz and a data rate up to 10 Gbit/s in visible light. Separately, the device achieves a responsivity of ~492 mA·W −1 and a near-unity external quantum efficiency of 95.6% at 638 nm. This combination of two-dimensional homostructure and TFLN nano-waveguides provides a basis for high-speed photodetectors and visible-light interconnections in future TFLN integrated optoelectronics and optical input/output applications.

Latitude modulates climate-driven maize yield gains across the central U.S. “warming hole”
works.abstract: Abstract Maize yield responses to climate change differ seasonally and regionally, with both positive and negative impacts shaped by local climate trends and management decisions. Here, using a phenology-aligned moving crop-season framework and the Hybrid-Maize model (1991–2024) across five U.S. Corn Belt states, we quantify climate-driven yield contributions and show that they transition from southern declines to northern gains, reflecting the persistent influence of the central U.S. summer warming hole characterized by cooling maximum temperatures and increasing rainfall. A systematic thermal mismatch between environmental heat availability and hybrid growing degree day requirements is observed, particularly south of 42°N, where thermal matching declined despite favorable thermal conditions. Contrasting trends in thermal matching and reproductive duration help explain the latitude-dependent structure of climate-driven yield contributions. Our findings highlight how hybrid selection modulates the impacts of temperature, precipitation, vapor pressure deficit, and radiation trends on maize yield gains across the U.S. Corn Belt.

ISG15 promotes PARP inhibitor resistance in BRCA1-deficient cells by facilitating DNA replication and repair
works.abstract: Abstract The use of poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPi) has proven largely successful in targeting BRCA1/2 -mutated tumours. However, the emergence of PARPi-resistant disease can reduce the efficacy of this treatment, posing significant challenges in the clinic. Here, we use multiple models of BRCA1 -/- cells and patient-derived xenografts (PDXs) that have been treated with PARPi until they no longer responded to the drug, to characterise genomic and transcriptomic alterations specific to PARPi resistance. We find that abrogation of TP53BP1 expression occurs spontaneously during prolonged PARPi treatment, alongside TP53BP1 genomic deletions and promoter methylation. Additionally, innate immune response genes, including ISG15 and factors of the ISGylation machinery are upregulated in PARPi-resistant cells and tumours. We demonstrate that ISG15 inhibition re-sensitises PARPi-resistant cells to the drug and, conversely, that ISG15 overexpression in BRCA1 -/- cells promotes PARPi resistance. Mechanistically, BRCA1 -/- PARPi-resistant cells rely on ISG15 for replication fork progression and restart of stalled forks and for DNA double-strand break (DSB) repair via homologous recombination (HR). Our results indicate that complex ISG15 interactions with DNA replication/repair factors can drive PARPi resistance in BRCA1-deficient cancer cells and that targeting ISG15 has the potential to overcome PARPi resistance.

works.title: Category learning drives cortical attentional gain to diagnostic dimensions of perceptual information
works.abstract: Humans and other animals develop remarkable perceptual and cognitive specializations for identifying, differentiating, and acting on classes of ecologically important signals. This expertise is flexible enough to support diverse perceptual judgments: a voice, for example, simultaneously conveys what a talker says, as well as myriad cues about her identity and state. Expert perception across complex signals thus involves discovering and learning regularities that best inform diverse perceptual judgments, as well as weighting this information flexibly as task demands change. Here, we test whether this process may involve attentional gain. We use two prospective auditory category learning tasks to relate a complex, entirely novel soundscape to four classes of ‘alien identity’ and two classes of ‘alien size.’ Identity, but not size, categorization requires discovery and learning of patterned acoustic input situated in one of two simultaneous, non-overlapping frequency bands. This allows us to capitalize on the coarsely segregated, frequency-band-specific channels tiling auditory cortex. We use fMRI to ask whether category-relevant perceptual information present in one frequency band is prioritized relative to simultaneous, uninformative information in the other frequency band. Only among participants expert at alien identity categorization do we observe neural prioritization of the identity-diagnostic frequency band. This prioritization persists even when the diagnostic information becomes irrelevant in the size categorization task. Tellingly, the neural selectivity evoked implicitly in the identity categorization task aligns with that in an independent task, where activation is driven by explicit and sustained selective attention to pure tones in one or the other frequency band. Additionally, the learning trajectories taken to achieve expert-level categorization leave fingerprints on the patterns of neural activity associated with the diagnostic dimension. In all, this indicates that learning categories can drive attentional gain to category-diagnostic input dimensions.

works.title: Neural integration of acoustic statistics enables mice to detect acoustic targets in noise
works.abstract: Sound detection amidst noise presents an important challenge in audition. Many naturally occurring sounds (rain, wind) can be described and predicted only statistically, so-called sound textures. Previous research has demonstrated the human ability to leverage this statistical predictability for sound recognition, but the neural mechanisms remain elusive. We trained mice to detect vocalizations embedded in sound textures with different statistical predictability, while recording and optogenetically modulating the neural activity in the auditory cortex. Mice showed improved performance and neural encoding if they could sample the statistics longer per trial. Textures with more exploitable structure, specifically higher cross-frequency correlations improved behavioral performance as well as neural representation of vocalizations. Activating parvalbumin-positive (PV) interneurons had an asymmetric effect depending on the acoustic context, improving detection and neural encoding of vocalizations for low correlations, and impoverishing them for high cross-frequency correlations. In summary, mice exploit stimulus statistics to improve sound detection in naturalistic background noise, reflected in behavioral performance and neural activity, relying on PV interneurons for temporal integration.

works.title: Life-cycle plasticity enables conditional asexual reproduction in a kelp
works.abstract: Many organisms alternate between distinct life stages and can reproduce either sexually or asexually, yet the mechanisms coordinating these developmental and reproductive transitions remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate the molecular basis of life stage identity and reproductive mode in the kelp Laminaria pallida , a multicellular organism with a complex life cycle. By combining gene expression analyses with developmental experiments and natural population-level approaches, we characterize the transcriptional signatures associated with developmental state transitions in both sexual and asexual contexts. We show that asexual reproduction is associated with endoreduplication and reduced fitness, while it is retained but rarely expressed in two natural populations. Moreover, we find that the presence of potential mating partners reduces asexual development, revealing that reproductive mode is adjusted in response to reproductive opportunities. Together, these findings suggest that asexual reproduction functions as a conditional alternative to sex, promoting persistence when sexual reproduction is constrained while preserving the long-term benefits of sexual reproduction when mates are available. More broadly, our results reveal how organisms integrate developmental, environmental, and reproductive cues to balance alternative reproductive strategies across complex life cycles.

works.title: The importance of genes does not predict their mutation rate
works.abstract: The convention that mutation is a random process has been challenged by suggestions that selection has acted on between-gene variation in the mutation rate, with claims that more important genes are protected from mutation in part, in prokaryotes, by being on the leading strand, while those required for rapid adaptive evolution have higher mutation rates, in part by being on the lagging strand. The original selectionist claims have proven contentious with several replication failures. However, none of the replication attempts fully allow for covariates and many employ data from mismatch repair (MMR) knockout strains. To address these limitations, we consider amassed mutation accumulation data for wild-type Escherichia coli , the focal species for adaptive claims, and Saccharomyces cerevisiae , in a multiple parameter-controlled analysis to predict between-gene variation in mutational density (mutations per base pair). Along with covariates, we consider putative selectively relevant parameters: protein level and essentiality to capture genic “importance”, and, in E. coli , strand with respect to DNA replication. We consider deviation of correlation and partial correlation values from those expected under trinucleotide-controlled simulations. While in E. coli more highly transcribed genes may have slightly lower mutation rates, potentially consistent with a selectionist model, the same is not seen in yeast, and in neither species do genes for more abundant or essential proteins have lower mutation rates. In E. coli there is no difference in mutation rate between genes on different strands, a lack of difference replicated in other prokaryotes. The degree of purifying selection is also not predictive of mutation density. We additionally highlight a strong artefact seen using the standard off-the-shelf statistical approach and note that results from MMR-deficient strains are discordant. We conclude that as trends are nearly uniformly unsupportive, not consistent between species and of miniscule effect size, they present no challenge to convention.

works.title: Learning-associated flexibility of cortical taste coding is impaired in Shank3 knockout mice
works.abstract: The ability to update the valence of sensory perception to influence behavior is crucial for survival. A common phenotype in autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) is defects in sensory processing, but whether these defects impair flexible sensory encoding is largely unexplored. In particular, how genetic risk factors such as Shank3 deletion affect the adaptability of cortical taste processing and downstream behavior is unknown. To address this gap, we performed two-photon calcium imaging during a conditioned taste aversion (CTA) learning paradigm, an ethologically relevant form of associative learning that depends on taste processing in the gustatory cortex (GC), to examine how Shank3 knockout alters taste-related neuronal activity in GC and influences CTA learning. We found that GC neurons in Shank3 knockout mice exhibited reduced stimulus-evoked suppression and increased trial-to-trial correlated variability during the acquisition of CTA memory. These activity changes, which likely reduced signal-to-noise ratio in GC, were associated with slower CTA acquisition in Shank3 knockout mice. In both genotypes, CTA learning enhanced, while subsequent extinction reduced, taste discriminability in GC, and both extinction and the associated reduction in discriminability were faster in Shank3 knockout than in wild-type mice. Together, these results show that Shank3 loss is associated with destabilized cortical activity dynamics in GC, which may contribute to inefficient encoding and maintenance of learned taste aversion. These findings show that loss of Shank3 compromises the ability of animals to update behavior to incorporate negative outcomes, and suggest this loss of flexibility may be an important feature of monogenic ASDs.

works.title: Cis-regulation and natural selection in the evolution of human DNA methylation
works.abstract: The vast collection of human-specific traits—such as our unique morphology, cognition, behavior, and diseases—has long been attributed to gene expression divergence between us and our closest living relatives, chimpanzees. Theory suggests that changes to cis -regulatory elements such as promoters and enhancers may drive evolutionary adaptation, and DNA methylation is a key factor in transcriptional cis -regulation. However, we still lack an understanding of (1) how species-specific methylation patterns arise; (2) their downstream effects; and (3) whether they are a common target of natural selection. In this study, we investigated these three questions. By combining a novel hypothesis testing framework with DNA methylation data from six human and chimpanzee cell types, as well as fused interspecies hybrid cells, we disentangled cis - vs. trans -acting methylation divergence across the genome. Across cell types, we found that methylation divergence is primarily driven in cis , which can be linked in some cases to nearby sequence variants such as CpG gains and losses. Although less common, regions with trans -acting methylation divergence were enriched for specific transcription factor (TF) binding motifs, suggesting a role of TFs such as FOXM1 in these differences. Having established these causes of methylation divergence, we then examined the functional consequences of differential methylation. Although methylation lacks a consistent relationship with transcription, we observed that associations between methylation and gene expression are stronger for genes with cis -regulatory divergence. Moreover, we identified lineage-specific selection shaping promoter methylation at the level of entire pathways, including those associated with human-specific traits such as speech, cognition, and susceptibility to infection with hepatitis C. Collectively, our findings provide a mechanistic framework suggesting that DNA methylation may occupy a key position, mediating the effects of both cis - and trans -acting factors on transcriptional networks, including those contributing to human-specific traits.
